warmup.q: A pipeline reads supplyAsync(this::fetchRate, io).thenApply(this::convert).thenApply(this::charge).exceptionally(ex -> fallback). fetchRate throws an IllegalStateException. What happens?
options: convert and charge run with a null rate
convert and charge are skipped, and exceptionally gets the exception wrapped in a CompletionException
supplyAsync throws the exception on the calling thread
convert and charge are skipped, and exceptionally gets the IllegalStateException itself
warmup.why: A failed stage skips every later thenApply until a handler. The handler sees a CompletionException with the IllegalStateException as its cause, because the exception was thrown inside a stage. The last option is the tempting one, and code that tests ex instanceof IllegalStateException there is silently wrong.

sections.h: A failure skips every step until a handler catches it
sections.html:
When a stage throws, its future completes exceptionally. Every thenApply, thenCompose and thenCombine after it is skipped: the function never runs, and its own future fails with the same cause. The failure travels down the chain until it reaches a handler. There are four:

Method Runs on Changes the outcome?
exceptionally(ex -> value) failure only yes, replaces the failure with a value
handle((value, ex) -> result) success and failure yes, returns any result
whenComplete((value, ex) -> ...) success and failure no, passes the outcome on
exceptionallyCompose(ex -> future) failure only yes, with another future (JDK 12)

Where you attach the handler decides what you recover. Put exceptionally at the end of a checkout and the conversion and charge steps are skipped; the only honest value left to return is "declined". Put it right after the FX call and it can return the last known rate, and every later step runs as if nothing went wrong. Recover as close to the failing call as you can, with a value that makes sense at that point.

whenComplete is for logs and metrics. It sees both outcomes and hands the same one on. One detail: if its action throws after a success, the result becomes that failure; after a failure, the original failure wins.

When the fallback is itself asynchronous, such as a second FX provider or a cache service with an async client, use exceptionallyCompose. It is to exceptionally what thenCompose is to thenApply:

Java
CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = live.rateAsync(pair)
        .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> backup.rateAsync(pair));   // JDK 12+
Kotlin
val rate: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = live.rateAsync(pair)
    .exceptionallyCompose { backup.rateAsync(pair) }       // JDK 12+

try.title: Move the handler
steps: Run ErrorPathDemo. The FX call throws. Before you run it, write down which of the numbered steps will print.
Run it with -Pargs=early, which recovers the rate right after the call. Predict again, including what whenComplete sees.

code.title: ErrorPathDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.math.RoundingMode; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** The FX call fails. Which steps still run? Pass "early" to recover the rate right after the call. */ public class ErrorPathDemo { static BigDecimal liveRate() { throw new IllegalStateException("FX provider returned 502"); } static <T> T step(String what, T value) { System.out.println(what); return value; } public static void main(String[] args) { boolean early = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("early"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(ErrorPathDemo::liveRate, io); if (early) { rate = rate.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover the rate itself System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return new BigDecimal("1.0800"); // the last known rate }); } CompletableFuture<String> result = rate .thenApply(r -> step("1. convert at " + r, new BigDecimal("100.00").multiply(r))) .thenApply(usd -> step("2. round to cents", usd.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN))) .thenApply(usd -> step("3. charge " + usd + " USD", "charged " + usd + " USD")) .whenComplete((v, ex) -> System.out.println("whenComplete sees: " + (ex == null ? v : ex))); if (!early) { result = result.exceptionally(ex -> { // recover at the end instead System.out.println("exceptionally sees: " + ex); return "declined: FX rate unavailable"; }); } System.out.println("result: " + result.join()); } } }

With early, exceptionally fires first, then steps 1, 2 and 3 run with the 1.0800 rate, and whenComplete sees charged 108.00 USD, a success.

sections.h: CompletionException: the wrapper you sometimes get
sections.html:
Handlers don't always see your exception. They see one of two things, by a rule that surprises everyone once.

If the exception was thrown inside a stage, by a supplyAsync task or a thenApply function, the future stores it wrapped in a CompletionException. A handler on that future, or on any later stage, gets the wrapper, with your exception as getCause().

If someone completed the future with completeExceptionally(ex), as orTimeout and many client libraries do, a handler attached directly to that future gets ex itself. One stage later it is wrapped again. The wrapper comes from the library catching your exception inside a stage; completeExceptionally stores exactly the exception it is given. WrapDemo prints all the cases:

1. handle() on the supplyAsync future      CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
2. handle() on completeExceptionally       IllegalStateException
3. handle() one stage later                CompletionException <- IllegalStateException
4. handle() after orTimeout                TimeoutException
5. get() throws                            ExecutionException <- IllegalStateException
6. join() throws                           CompletionException <- IllegalStateException

The last two lines are the blocking calls from the previous lesson: get() throws ExecutionException and join() throws CompletionException, both with the original as the cause.

So a handler that checks ex instanceof TimeoutException is right in one place and silently wrong one stage further down. Unwrap first, then decide:

Java
.exceptionally(ex -> {
    Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null) ? ex.getCause() : ex;
    if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return lastKnownRate;
    throw new CompletionException(cause);       // not ours to handle: keep failing
})
Kotlin
.exceptionally { ex ->
    val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex
    if (cause is TimeoutException) lastKnownRate
    else throw CompletionException(cause)       // not ours to handle: keep failing
}

Rethrowing inside a handler is how you say "I looked, and this one isn't mine". The lab's unwrap does the same job in a loop, and also strips the ExecutionException that get() adds. On a completed future, exceptionNow() (JDK 19) hands you the unwrapped cause directly.

try.title: Predict the wrapper
steps: Cover the output above. Read WrapDemo and write down, for each numbered line, what you expect it to print.
Run it and check. For each line you got wrong, find whether the exception was thrown inside a stage or passed to completeExceptionally.

code.title: WrapDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CompletionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** Which exception does each handler see? Predict every line before you run it. */ public class WrapDemo { static String describe(Throwable ex) { String name = ex.getClass().getSimpleName(); return ex.getCause() == null ? name : name + " <- " + ex.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName(); } static void show(String label, CompletableFuture<?> f) { String seen = f.handle((v, ex) -> describe(ex)).join(); System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", label, seen); } public static void main(String[] args) { IllegalStateException down = new IllegalStateException("502"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<String> supplied = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { throw down; }, io); CompletableFuture<String> completed = new CompletableFuture<>(); completed.completeExceptionally(down); CompletableFuture<String> timedOut = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> sleepThen(1000, "late"), io) .orTimeout(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); show("1. handle() on the supplyAsync future", supplied); show("2. handle() on completeExceptionally", completed); show("3. handle() one stage later", completed.thenApply(String::trim)); show("4. handle() after orTimeout", timedOut); try { supplied.get(); } catch (ExecutionException | InterruptedException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "5. get() throws", describe(e)); } try { supplied.join(); } catch (CompletionException e) { System.out.printf("%-42s %s%n", "6. join() throws", describe(e)); } } } static String sleepThen(long ms, String value) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return value; } }

sections.h: Timeouts end the wait, not the work
sections.html:
JDK 9 added two timeouts to CompletableFuture:

Java
quote.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);                    // fails with TimeoutException
quote.completeOnTimeout(lastKnown, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // completes with a default
Kotlin
quote.orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                     // fails with TimeoutException
quote.completeOnTimeout(lastKnown, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)  // completes with a default

Both change the future you call them on and return it. If it hasn't completed when the time is up, a JDK timer thread completes it (on JDK 21 the thread is called CompletableFutureDelayScheduler). Plain stages attached to it then run on that timer thread, so keep them cheap.

What neither one does is touch the task. The provider call keeps running on its io thread until it returns, and then its result is thrown away. KeepsRunningDemo gives a 600 ms call a 200 ms timeout: the future fails at 200 ms, and the call finishes at 600 ms anyway.

cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture is no better. Its Javadoc says the mayInterruptIfRunning flag "has no effect in this implementation because interrupts are not used to control processing." The future completes with CancellationException and the task runs on. That is the opposite of the FutureTask from submit, where cancel(true) interrupts the worker, as lesson 4 of this track showed.

This matters under load. Take a 20-thread pool and a provider that hangs for 30 seconds. Each request gets its TimeoutException after 300 ms, right on time, but each call holds its thread for 30 seconds. After 20 requests the pool is full of calls nobody is waiting for, and new calls, even to healthy providers, queue behind them and time out too.

So every remote call needs two timeouts. The one on the future is the caller's deadline. The one in the client (the HTTP client's request timeout, the JDBC query timeout) gives the thread back. Set the client's timeout no longer than the future's, and bound the pool per provider, as lesson 3 of this track did with bulkheads.

Pass "cancel" to try cancel(true) at 200 ms instead. */ public class KeepsRunningDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %-31s %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, Thread.currentThread().getName(), msg); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean cancel = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("cancel"); try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> quote = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { log("asking the slow provider"); try { Thread.sleep(600); } catch (InterruptedException e) { log("interrupted: the call stops here"); throw new IllegalStateException(e); } log("provider answered, but nobody is listening"); return new BigDecimal("1.0842"); }, io); if (cancel) { Thread.sleep(200); log("cancel(true) returned " + quote.cancel(true)); } else { quote.orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); } quote.handle((v, ex) -> { log("the future completed with " + (ex == null ? v : ex.getClass().getSimpleName())); return null; }).join(); } // close() waits for the provider call, which is still running log("pool closed"); } }

With cancel, cancel(true) returns true and the future completes with CancellationException on main, but the line interrupted never prints: the call runs to 600 ms.

sections.h: Fan-out: allOf waits for everyone, anyOf takes whoever finishes first
sections.html:
To ask three FX providers at once, start three futures and combine them. The JDK gives you two combinators, and neither does what you want on its own.

allOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Void>. It completes when all three have completed, and it has no results of its own: you read them from your futures with join(), which no longer blocks because they're all done. If any of them failed, allOf fails too, but only after the slowest one finishes. One provider that returns a 503 in 50 ms fails the whole call, 300 ms later.

anyOf(f1, f2, f3) returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes like whichever future completes first. That includes a failure. A provider that fails fast beats two that answer correctly a little later. If what you want is the first successful answer, anyOf can't give it to you; the deeper section has a ten-line helper for that.

The fix is to make each call unable to fail before you combine them. Give every call its own timeout, then turn any failure into "no answer":

Java
CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> safe = ask(provider)
        .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                       // this provider's deadline
        .handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.empty());
Kotlin
val safe: CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>> = ask(provider)
    .orTimeout(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)                          // this provider's deadline
    .handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() }

Now allOf over the safe futures can only succeed, and the step after it picks the best answer, or fails with a clear error when every provider was skipped. The timeout must sit on each call. Put one orTimeout on the allOf instead and one hung provider throws away the two good answers.

That is the lab: a quote aggregator with a timeout per provider, a report for every skipped provider with its real cause, and the lowest price among those that answered.

try.title: Three ways to fan out
steps: Read FanOutDemo: flaky fails at 50 ms, alpha answers at 100 ms, beta at 300 ms.
Run it with -Pargs=any, then -Pargs=all, then -Pargs=safe. Before each run, predict the result and when it arrives.

code.title: FanOutDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l07; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.List; import java.util.Optional; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** flaky fails at 50 ms, alpha answers at 100 ms, beta at 300 ms. Pass any, all or safe. */ public class FanOutDemo { static final long T0 = System.nanoTime(); static void log(String msg) { System.out.printf("%4d ms %s%n", (System.nanoTime() - T0) / 1_000_000, msg); } static CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> ask(String name, long ms, String price, ExecutorService io) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> { sleep(ms); if (price == null) { log(name + " fails"); throw new IllegalStateException(name + " returned 503"); } log(name + " answers " + price); return new BigDecimal(price); }, io); } public static void main(String[] args) { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "all"; try (ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory())) { List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> asks = List.of( ask("flaky", 50, null, io), ask("alpha", 100, "1.0850", io), ask("beta", 300, "1.0842", io)); CompletableFuture<?> result = switch (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure case "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)); // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed case "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> asks.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail default -> { List<CompletableFuture<Optional<BigDecimal>>> safe = asks.stream() .map(f -> f.handle((price, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(price) : Optional.<BigDecimal>empty())) .toList(); yield CompletableFuture.allOf(safe.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) .thenApply(done -> safe.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).flatMap(Optional::stream) .min(Comparator.naturalOrder()).orElseThrow()); } }; result.handle((v, ex) -> { log(mode + ": " + (ex == null ? "result " + v : "failed with " + ex.getCause())); return null; }).join(); } } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

Pass any, all or safe. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "all" Executors.newFixedThreadPool(3, Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 1).factory()).use { io -> val asks = listOf(ask("flaky", 50, null, io), ask("alpha", 100, "1.0850", io), ask("beta", 300, "1.0842", io)) val result: CompletableFuture<*> = when (mode) { // the first future to complete wins, even when it completes with a failure "any" -> CompletableFuture.anyOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) // waits for all three, then fails because one of them failed "all" -> CompletableFuture.allOf(*asks.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { asks.map { it.join() }.min() } // turn each failure into an empty Optional first, so allOf can't fail else -> { val safe = asks.map { f -> f.handle { price, ex -> if (ex == null) Optional.of(price) else Optional.empty() } } CompletableFuture.allOf(*safe.toTypedArray()) .thenApply { safe.mapNotNull { it.join().orElse(null) }.min() } } } result.handle { v, ex -> log("$mode: " + if (ex == null) "result $v" else "failed with ${ex.cause}") }.join() } }

try.expect: any fails at about 50 ms with flaky's 503, and alpha and beta keep running after the result is printed. all also fails with the 503, but only at about 300 ms, after beta answers. safe succeeds at about 300 ms with 1.0842, beta's price, because the failure became an empty Optional. Timestamps run a bit late on a busy machine.

analogy: You phone three exchange bureaus for a EUR/USD rate. allOf is waiting until all three have called back, and giving up on the whole thing if one of them called to say it's closed. anyOf is taking whoever calls back first, even if that call is to say they're closed. The safe pattern gives each call its own egg timer: when it rings, you write "no answer" next to that bureau, and when every line has a rate or a "no answer", you pick the best rate. The analogy breaks when you hang up. A clerk who hears you hang up stops working. A provider call in the JVM keeps running after your timeout, and it keeps a pool thread busy until it's done.
world: Authorization paths are full of fan-outs with deadlines: a fraud vendor that must answer in 150 ms or the payment goes to manual review, an issuer call with a 2 s budget, two FX providers where any recent rate will do. Give each dependency its own deadline and its own fallback, close to the call, and record which path each request took with whenComplete, so a dashboard shows when the fallback rate becomes the normal rate. Remember the second timeout in the client, or a slow vendor quietly fills your pool. Temporal's activity timeouts have the same limit one level up: when an activity times out, the worker keeps running the activity code until it heartbeats and learns it was cancelled. In Quarkus, MicroProfile Fault Tolerance's @Timeout and @Fallback do this job with annotations, and the same two-timeout question applies.
mistake: The common mistake is putting orTimeout on the future and thinking the slow call is handled. The caller does get its answer on time, so every test passes. In production a hung provider keeps each abandoned call on a pool thread for as long as the HTTP client is willing to wait, often 30 seconds or more. The pool fills with calls nobody is waiting for, and requests to healthy providers start timing out behind them. People make the mistake because the future and the work feel like one thing. They aren't: the future is a box for the answer. Set a client-side timeout no longer than the future's deadline, and give each provider its own bounded pool or semaphore.

compare.title: One provider call with a deadline: CompletableFuture vs coroutines

java.title: Ask.java (CompletableFuture)
java.html: CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>> ask(QuoteProvider p, String pair) { return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> new Quote(p.name(), p.quote(pair)), io) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // the caller stops waiting... .handle((q, ex) -> ex == null ? Optional.of(q) : Optional.empty()); // ...but p.quote keeps running on io until it returns }

kotlin.title: Ask.kt (kotlinx.coroutines)
kotlin.html: suspend fun ask(p: QuoteProvider, pair: String): Quote? = try { withTimeoutOrNull(300.milliseconds) { // null when time is up runInterruptible(Dispatchers.IO) { // interrupts the thread on cancel Quote(p.name(), p.quote(pair)) } } } catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e // never swallow cancellation } catch (e: Exception) { null // a failure becomes "no answer" }

compare.note: The shapes match: a deadline, then a failure turned into "no answer". The difference is what happens to the work. orTimeout only completes the future, and the provider call runs to its end. withTimeoutOrNull cancels the block, and runInterruptible turns that cancellation into Thread.interrupt() on the IO thread, so a blocking call that responds to interrupts stops and gives its thread back. In both languages, a call that ignores interrupts keeps its thread, which is why the client-side timeout still matters. Kotlin also makes you rethrow CancellationException by hand when you catch Exception; CompletableFuture has no such trap.

worked.title: Give the FX call a deadline and a fallback

steps.say: The checkout gets its rate from an async FX client. When the provider hangs, every checkout hangs with it. Before reading on, decide what should happen after 300 ms.
steps.code: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair) { return fx.rateAsync(pair); // no deadline: a hung provider hangs the checkout }

alt.html: fun rate(pair: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = fx.rateAsync(pair) // no deadline: a hung provider hangs the checkout

steps.say: Give the live call a deadline, observe failures without changing them, then fall back to the rate cache, which has its own async client. The cache gets its own short deadline, because exceptionallyCompose starts a new call that the first timeout doesn't cover.
steps.code: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair) { return fx.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the live call gets 300 ms .whenComplete((r, ex) -> { // 2. observe, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("fx.live.failed", unwrap(ex).getClass().getSimpleName()); }) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> cache.rateAsync(pair) // 3. fall back, asynchronously .orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)); // 4. the fallback's own deadline }

alt.html: fun rate(pair: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = fx.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 1. the live call gets 300 ms .whenComplete { _, ex -> // 2. observe, don't change if (ex != null) metrics.count("fx.live.failed", unwrap(ex).javaClass.simpleName) } .exceptionallyCompose { // 3. fall back, asynchronously cache.rateAsync(pair).orTimeout(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) // 4. the fallback's own deadline }

steps.say: Why unwrap in the metric? The live client may complete its future with a raw exception, orTimeout stores a raw TimeoutException, and anything thrown inside a stage arrives wrapped. Without unwrapping, half your failures would be tagged CompletionException, which tells the on-call engineer nothing.

One gap is left. After 300 ms the checkout moves on, but the live call still holds a thread and a connection. Give the HTTP request a timeout of its own, so the client gives up too. With the JDK client it is one line on the request.
steps.code: HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the client stops waiting too .build();

alt.html: val request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri) .timeout(Duration.ofMillis(300)) // 5. the client stops waiting too .build()

lab.title: A quote aggregator that survives bad providers
steps: Run the tests. All seven fail. Read the Javadoc on QuoteAggregator: it is the spec.
Write unwrap: loop while the throwable is a CompletionException or an ExecutionException and has a cause, moving to the cause each time.

Add a private method ask(QuoteProvider p, String pair) that returns CompletableFuture<Optional<Quote>>: supplyAsync on io, then orTimeout, then handle. On failure, call onSkip.accept(p.name(), unwrap(ex)) and return Optional.empty().

In best, map every provider to ask, collect the futures in a list, and allOf them. In the thenApply after it, join each future, keep the present quotes, and return the lowest price, or throw NoQuoteException.
Run the tests until all seven pass, then once more.
hints: orTimeout takes a long and a unit: orTimeout(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).
allOf takes an array (asks.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)) and returns CompletableFuture<Void>. Read the quotes from your own list.
If skipsFailingProvider reports a CompletionException, you passed ex to onSkip without unwrapping it. If skipsSlowProvider times out, the deadline is on the whole call, not on each provider.
Throwing NoQuoteException inside the thenApply is enough: the returned future fails with it as the cause.

drill.title: A rate with a deadline and a fallback
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair): call live.rateAsync(pair) with a 300 ms deadline; if it fails for any reason, log the unwrapped cause and fall back to backup.rateAsync(pair), which returns a CompletableFuture too. Then compare. Which method did you use for the fallback, and did you unwrap before logging?

answer.title: Rates.java
answer.html: CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> rate(String pair) { return live.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .exceptionallyCompose(ex -> { Throwable cause = ex instanceof CompletionException && ex.getCause() != null ? ex.getCause() : ex; log.warn("live FX failed, using backup: {}", cause.toString()); return backup.rateAsync(pair); // a future, so exceptionallyCompose, not exceptionally }); }

alt.title: Rates.kt
alt.html: fun rate(pair: String): CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> = live.rateAsync(pair) .orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) .exceptionallyCompose { ex -> val cause = if (ex is CompletionException && ex.cause != null) ex.cause!! else ex log.warn("live FX failed, using backup: {}", cause.toString()) backup.rateAsync(pair) // a future, so exceptionallyCompose, not exceptionally }

recap: A failure skips every later stage until a handler. exceptionally and handle can recover, whenComplete only observes, exceptionallyCompose (JDK 12) recovers with another future.
Exceptions thrown inside a stage reach handlers wrapped in CompletionException. completeExceptionally and orTimeout store them raw. Unwrap before you test the type.
orTimeout and completeOnTimeout end the caller's wait, not the work. cancel(true) on a CompletableFuture doesn't interrupt either. Give the client its own timeout.
allOf waits for every future and fails if any failed. anyOf takes the first to complete, failures included.
For a fan-out, give each call its own timeout and turn its failure into "no answer" before allOf, then pick from what came back.

explain.prompt: A teammate's quote aggregator does allOf(askA, askB, askC).orTimeout(500, MILLISECONDS) and then picks the lowest price. Explain why it fails whenever one provider is down or slow, and how you would restructure it.
explain.answer: allOf fails if any of its futures fails, so one provider returning an error fails the whole call, and it only fails after the slowest provider finishes. The single orTimeout on the allOf means one hung provider makes the whole call time out and throws away the answers that did come back. I'd give each provider call its own orTimeout, then a handle that turns a failure into an empty Optional and reports the unwrapped cause. Then allOf over those safe futures can't fail, and the step after it picks the lowest price from the ones that are present, or fails with a clear "no quote" error if all are empty. I'd also set a timeout in the HTTP client, because orTimeout doesn't stop the call itself.

deeper.html:
anyOf gives you the first to finish, not the first to succeed. When you want the first success, complete a future of your own from each success, and fail it only when every call has failed. complete returns false for every caller after the first, so the first success wins without a lock:

Java
static <T> CompletableFuture<T> firstSuccess(List<CompletableFuture<T>> calls) {   // calls must not be empty
    CompletableFuture<T> first = new CompletableFuture<>();
    AtomicInteger failed = new AtomicInteger();
    for (CompletableFuture<T> call : calls) {
        call.whenComplete((value, ex) -> {
            if (ex == null) first.complete(value);                                   // only the first one counts
            else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size()) first.completeExceptionally(ex);
        });
    }
    return first;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> firstSuccess(calls: List<CompletableFuture<T>>): CompletableFuture<T> {     // calls must not be empty
    val first = CompletableFuture<T>()
    val failed = AtomicInteger()
    for (call in calls) {
        call.whenComplete { value, ex ->
            if (ex == null) first.complete(value)                                    // only the first one counts
            else if (failed.incrementAndGet() == calls.size) first.completeExceptionally(ex)
        }
    }
    return first
}

Two smaller things are worth knowing. orTimeout and completeOnTimeout change the very future you call them on. If a client library hands the same cached future to several callers, one caller's timeout fails it for all of them. Call copy() (JDK 9) first and put the timeout on your copy. And when you need a delay without a timeout, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io) (JDK 9) returns an Executor that runs each task 500 ms after you submit it. It is handy for a retry with backoff: supplyAsync(this::call, CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, MILLISECONDS, io)).
